title: Our Publications
text: Our Publications All Working Papers Policy Papers AI Innovation Employment France Europe Democracy Policy Paper · October 2026 Innovation and catch-up in the AI model market Paul Delbouve LIFT Policy Paper 2026-04 — October 2026 AI Innovation Competition In AI, the best model sold for 0.1 dollar per million tokens or less, at least fifty times cheaper than a frontier model, catches up with its quality in less than a year. This catch-up could discourage growing investment, on the order of 715 billion dollars in 2026 for the main AI developers, by reducing the rent that a technological lead provides. On OpenRouter, frontier labs handle only 28% of tokens in August 2026, compared with three quarters in spring 2025, but still collect 71% of revenue thanks to higher prices. Relative to its competitors, a provider that releases a frontier model sees its imputed revenue roughly double in the following months, and the users of a model facing new competition mostly switch to other high-end models. This equilibrium rests on exceptional growth in consumption and remains fragile: frontier labs’ share of revenue fell from 82% to 71% between mid-July and mid-August 2026. Abstract ↓ Read → PDF in French ↓ Policy Paper · October 2026 Rising AI spending and the rise of open-weight models Antonin Bergeaud , Paul Delbouve , Etienne Grass LIFT Policy Paper 2026-03 — October 2026 AI France Open models Firms’ AI spending is rising even as the unit cost of a token falls sharply: the increase comes from volumes far more than from prices. On OpenRouter, the share of open-weight models rises from 40% to 73% of tokens between January and August 2026, and from 11% to 34% of spending. Users attributed to France devote 31.0% of their spending to open models, compared with 19.3% worldwide. Calls to open models are four times longer than in January, but their average cost is only 3.8 times higher: the cost advantage persists. Reallocation toward open models accounts for 43% of the simulated decline in the cost of a constant French basket; it opens room for wider deployment rather than an automatic saving, which invites organizations to reason in terms of cost per completed task. Abstract ↓ Read → PDF in French ↓ Policy Paper · October 2026 Generative AI: a freeze on youth hiring in exposed occupations Antonin Bergeaud , Antoine Bertheau, Simon Bunel , Oscar Degos , Marco Guido Palladino LIFT Policy Paper 2026-02 — October 2026 AI France Employment Labor market Since November 2022, hires of 21-29-year-olds on open-ended contracts have fallen by 28.3% in the occupations most exposed to generative AI, compared with 7.5% in the least exposed. Separations are also falling, but less than hires: worker turnover is slowing and the market is freezing for young people in exposed occupations. The gap narrows with age, from more than 20 percentage points among 21-29-year-olds to less than 4 points after age 50, and it persists when fixed-term contracts are added to open-ended ones. It is not driven by developers alone, whose hires of young people on open-ended contracts fall by 42%: without them, the gap remains 17 points. Firms that report intensive use of AI hire relatively fewer young people, while their total headcount does not clearly diverge from that of other firms. The analysis covers labor turnover data from January 2019 to March 2026, matched with the Banque de France business survey, with which this work was carried out. The method and the full set of results are detailed in LIFT Working Paper 2026-02. Abstract ↓ Read → PDF in French ↓ Working Paper · October 2026 Occupational exposure to generative AI, firm adoption and labor market dynamics in France Marco Guido Palladino , Antonin Bergeaud , Antoine Bertheau, Simon Bunel , Oscar Degos LIFT Working Paper 2026-02 — October 2026 AI France Employment Labor market This paper studies how employment in France evolves with occupations’ exposure to generative artificial intelligence and with workers’ age. We build a new index that ranks occupations from least to most exposed, then draw on comprehensive administrative data on hires and separations between January 2019 and March 2026. Since November 2022, the month of ChatGPT’s public launch, both hires and separations on open-ended contracts have fallen more in the most exposed occupations, especially among young people. These trends point to a kind of freeze in labor turnover for new entrants in exposed occupations, with fewer entries and fewer exits. The result also holds among firms that report intensive use of AI: their hiring of young people on open-ended contracts declines relative to other firms, with no clear divergence in the evolution of their total employment compared with other firms. The main results are presented in short form in LIFT Policy Paper 2026-02. Abstract ↓ Read → PDF in French ↓ Policy Paper · September 2026 Why AI is not (yet) making France more productive Antonin Bergeaud , Simon Bunel LIFT Policy Paper 2026-01 — September 2026 AI France Productivity France spends as much as the United States on information technology (6.5% of GDP in 2025, compared with 6.8%), but its hourly productivity has stagnated since 2015: its lag stems from the return on this spending. Upstream, it is at the European average for research, patents and capital, but its computing power per capita is more than 50% below the European average. The French use generative AI individually at least as much as other Europeans, but their firms integrate it less: only 18% use it, compared with 26% in Germany, and integration remains shallow, concentrated in product development rather than in cross-cutting functions. This lag is above all organizational: 69% of French workers receive neither encouragement, nor tools, nor training in AI from their employer, compared with 44% in the United States. Abstract ↓ Read → PDF in French ↓ Working Paper · February 2026 Politics at work: workplace experience and political divides among employees in France Yann Algan , Antonin Bergeaud , Camille Frouard LIFT Working Paper 2026-01 — February 2026 (first released as an HEC Policy Note) Democracy Work France Politics Drawing on a survey of 3,900 private-sector employees in 2024-2025, this note analyzes how everyday experience at work shapes political divides in France. The axis that separates electorates at work is neither wages nor socio-occupational category, but the quality of the social ties experienced day to day in the firm. Employees close to the Rassemblement National (RN) show strong trust in their firm but distrust their colleagues and are socially isolated, while employees close to La France insoumise (LFI) distrust management but trust their colleagues. One third of employees, the most isolated at work, are unaffiliated and do not vote: disengagement at work precedes civic disengagement. Abstract ↓ Read → PDF in French ↓ Working Paper · October 2025 Cost of Failure, Disruptive Innovation and Targeted Flexicurity Yann Coatanlem, Oliver Coste LIFT Working Paper 2025-03 — October 2025 Innovation Europe Labor market This paper expands earlier work by assembling a larger sample of restructuring plans (250 plans) to measure the restructuring costs borne by large firms and to assess their links with business R&D in disruptive sectors (tech/biotech). The authors confirm a wide transatlantic gap, with Germany at 31 months of average salary versus 7 months in the United States, and identify low-cost outliers within Europe (Denmark, Switzerland). They show a strong negative correlation between restructuring costs and R&D intensity in tech and biotech, and conclude with recommendations for targeted reforms of employment protection laws that preserve social protection while restoring the agility critical for disruptive innovation. Abstract ↓ Read → PDF ↓ Working Paper · July 2025 Artificial intelligence in the service of innovation: an analysis of patent data Antonin Bergeaud LIFT Working Paper 2025-02 — July 2025 AI Innovation The impact of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies on economic growth depends largely on their ability to increase research productivity. In this article, we propose an original measure of the diffusion of AI across technologies, based on patents filed in the United States since 1990. Our methodology identifies patents that incorporate AI through their references to academic publications classified as AI. As of December 2024, about 5% of patents filed can thus be characterized as using AI. This approach captures the integration of AI into other technological fields, consistent with its nature as a general-purpose technology. We show that these “AI” patents systematically display higher quality indicators than other patents, according to several standard metrics. Abstract ↓ Read → PDF in French ↓ Working Paper · July 2025 The diffusion of artificial intelligence in France Philippe Aghion , Antonin Bergeaud , Simon Bunel , Paul Delbouve LIFT Working Paper 2025-01 — July 2025 AI France Tracker Employment Using more than 120 million job postings published online in France since 2019, this study examines the characteristics of the diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI) in firms and its effects on employment. AI diffusion turns out to be highly heterogeneous: it is particularly advanced in certain sectors (IT, finance, consulting) and within large pioneering firms. We show that the firms most exposed to AI were significantly more inclined to hire AI specialists as soon as ChatGPT appeared. At the same time, we observe a relative decline in job creation in the occupations most exposed to AI, but an increase in labor productivity in the firms concerned. Abstract ↓ Read → PDF in French ↓ Working Paper · January 2024 Exposure to generative artificial intelligence and employment: an application to the French socio-occupational classification Antonin Bergeaud LIFT Working Paper 2024-01 — January 2024 AI France Employment This paper analyzes the exposure of French occupations to generative artificial intelligence through the socio-occupational classification. Drawing on O*NET data and a GPT-4 assessment protocol, it proposes two indices: substitutability and complementarity. The results reveal strong heterogeneity across occupations, with higher exposure for the most skilled occupations. This approach helps to better identify automation risks and complementarity opportunities, and underscores the need to account for adoption costs and endogenous transformations to anticipate impacts on employment. title: Team
text: Team Members Researchers, economists and experts of the Laboratory of Innovation and Future Transformations. Core members Co-director Antonin Bergeaud Associate professor at HEC Paris, research affiliate of the CEP/LSE, the CEPR and the Collège de France’s Innovation Lab. His research focuses on growth, productivity and innovation. Co-director Yann Algan Associate Dean of Pre-Experience Programs and professor of economics at HEC Paris. His research focuses on trust, well-being in organizations and the evaluation of public policy. Core member Clément Mazet-Sonilhac Assistant professor at Bocconi University, he will join HEC Paris on January 1, 2027. His research focuses on technological change and financial intermediation. Fellows Fellow Simon Bunel Administrator of INSEE, postdoctoral researcher at the INSEAD Stone Centre and adjunct professor at the ENS. His work focuses on the macroeconomic effects of AI. Fellow Flavio Calvino Senior economist at the OECD. His research analyzes the impact of digital technologies and AI on firm dynamics and productivity. Fellow Marco G. Palladino Senior economist at the Banque de France and adjunct professor at Sciences Po. His research focuses on the role of firms in wage setting and on the effects of AI on the labor market. Associate researchers Associate researcher Thomas Renault Professor of economics at Université Paris-Saclay. His research lies at the intersection of economics, finance and technology, using machine learning and semantic analysis tools. Associate researcher Éric Hazan Entrepreneur, investor and lecturer at HEC Paris and Sciences Po. His work explores how AI is transforming firms, work and European competitiveness. Associate researcher Pascal Saint-Amans Former director of the OECD Centre for Tax Policy and Administration. He teaches at HEC Paris and the University of Lausanne. Associate researcher Arnaud Dyèvre Assistant professor of economics at HEC Paris. His research focuses on growth, innovation and the role of public research in the diffusion of knowledge. PhD students PhD student Paul Delbouve PhD student in macroeconomics at PSE (EHESS) and researcher at the French Ministry of the Economy and Finance. He studies the diffusion of AI in the French economy. title: Antonin Bergeaud
text: Antonin Bergeaud Antonin Bergeaud Co-director Antonin Bergeaud is an associate professor in the Economics Department of HEC Paris and a research affiliate of the LSE’s Centre for Economic Performance, the CEPR and the Collège de France’s Innovation Lab. His research focuses on long-run growth, productivity dynamics and the role of innovation in the diffusion of knowledge. He received the 2025 Best Young Economist Prize (Le Monde / Cercle des économistes). title: Clément Mazet-Sonilhac
text: Clément Mazet-Sonilhac Clément Mazet-Sonilhac Core member Clément Mazet-Sonilhac is an assistant professor at Bocconi University and a research associate at the Collège de France’s Economics of Innovation Lab and at IGIER. He will join the Economics Department of HEC Paris as an assistant professor on January 1, 2027. Previously a research economist at the Banque de France, he received his PhD in economics from Sciences Po Paris in 2022. His research focuses on technological change and financial intermediation: he combines applied econometrics, structural modeling and machine learning to study innovation, climate change and poverty reduction. His work has been published in the American Economic Review , the Journal of International Economics and the Journal of Labor Economics . Personal page

title: Simon Bunel
text: Simon Bunel Simon Bunel Fellow Simon Bunel is an administrator of INSEE (the French national statistics institute), a postdoctoral researcher at the INSEAD Stone Centre for the Study of Wealth Inequality and an adjunct professor at the École normale supérieure. A research associate at the Collège de France’s Farhi Economics of Innovation Lab, he works on the evaluation of public innovation policies, the effects of technological change on employment and the macroeconomic consequences of artificial intelligence. He is a co-author of Le Pouvoir de la destruction créatrice (Odile Jacob, 2023) and contributed to the report of the Artificial Intelligence Commission submitted to the President of the Republic in 2024. title: Flavio Calvino
text: Flavio Calvino Flavio Calvino Fellow Flavio Calvino is a senior economist at the OECD, where he leads the “Firms, digital transformation and technology diffusion” team. His research analyzes the impact of innovation and digital technologies, including AI, on firm dynamics, employment and productivity. Personal page

title: Marco G. Palladino
text: Marco G. Palladino Marco G. Palladino Fellow Marco G. Palladino is a senior economist at the Banque de France and an adjunct professor at Sciences Po (School of Public Affairs). He is also a research affiliate of IZA@LISER and a member of the OECD’s LinkEED network. His research in labor economics uses matched employer-employee administrative data, in France and internationally, to study the role of firms in wage setting, employment protection and the use of fixed-term contracts. He also works on the effects of artificial intelligence on the labor market. Personal page Publications Generative AI: a freeze on youth hiring in exposed occupations Policy Paper — October 2026 PDF in French Occupational exposure to generative AI, firm adoption and labor market dynamics in France Working Paper — October 2026 PDF in French

title: Thomas Renault
text: Thomas Renault Thomas Renault Associate researcher Thomas Renault is a professor of economics at Université Paris-Saclay. His research lies at the intersection of economics, finance and data analysis. Personal page

title: Éric Hazan
text: Éric Hazan Éric Hazan Associate researcher Éric Hazan is an entrepreneur, investor and lecturer at HEC Paris and Sciences Po, specializing in the economic and social transformations brought about by artificial intelligence. After 17 years at McKinsey, he co-founded Ardabelle Capital. His work explores how AI is transforming firms, work and European competitiveness. He is notably a co-author of Faut-il encore décider ? , on decision-making in the age of AI.

title: Pascal Saint-Amans
text: Pascal Saint-Amans Pascal Saint-Amans Associate researcher From 2012 to 2022, Pascal Saint-Amans headed the OECD Centre for Tax Policy and Administration, where he led the international negotiations on the taxation of multinationals that resulted in the agreement on a global minimum tax. He teaches at HEC Paris and the University of Lausanne and is affiliated with Bruegel.

title: Arnaud Dyèvre
text: Arnaud Dyèvre Arnaud Dyèvre Associate researcher Arnaud Dyèvre is an assistant professor of economics at HEC Paris. His research focuses on growth, innovation and productivity differences across firms, with particular attention to the role of public research in the diffusion of knowledge. He holds a PhD from the London School of Economics and was a postdoctoral researcher at MIT. Personal page

title: Paul Delbouve
text: Paul Delbouve Paul Delbouve PhD student Paul Delbouve is a PhD student in macroeconomics at the Paris School of Economics (EHESS) and a researcher at the French Ministry of the Economy and Finance. His research focuses on the diffusion of artificial intelligence in the French economy, using job posting data to trace AI adoption across firms, sectors and occupations. title: Philippe Aghion
text: Philippe Aghion Philippe Aghion Scientific council Philippe Aghion is a professor at the Collège de France, where he holds the chair in Economics of Institutions, Innovation and Growth, a professor at INSEAD and a visiting professor at the London School of Economics. His research focuses on economic growth: with Peter Howitt, he developed the Schumpeterian growth paradigm, based on innovation and creative destruction. In 2025 he received the Nobel Prize in Economics, with Joel Mokyr and Peter Howitt, for his work on the impact of new technologies on growth. Publications The diffusion of artificial intelligence in France Working Paper — July 2025 PDF in French

title: Christophe Pérignon
text: Christophe Pérignon Christophe Pérignon Scientific council Christophe Pérignon is a professor of finance at HEC Paris, Associate Dean for Research and director of the GREGHEC laboratory (CNRS-HEC). He is co-scientific director of Hi! PARIS and holds the Deloitte “AI for Business Innovation” chair. His research focuses on the applications and implications of artificial intelligence in finance. He co-founded cascad, an agency that certifies the reproducibility of scientific results. He received his PhD from the Swiss Finance Institute and taught at Simon Fraser University before joining HEC Paris in 2007. Personal page

The result also holds among firms that report intensive use of AI: their hiring of young people on open-ended contracts declines relative to other firms, with no clear divergence in the evolution of their total employment compared with other firms. The main results are presented in short form in LIFT Policy Paper 2026-02. PDF in French

title: Why AI is not (yet) making France more productive
text: Why AI is not (yet) making France more productive LIFT Policy Paper 2026-01 — September 2026 AI France Productivity Published September 2026 Abstract France spends as much as the United States on information technology (6.5% of GDP in 2025, compared with 6.8%), but its hourly productivity has stagnated since 2015: its lag stems from the return on this spending. Upstream, it is at the European average for research, patents and capital, but its computing power per capita is more than 50% below the European average. The French use generative AI individually at least as much as other Europeans, but their firms integrate it less: only 18% use it, compared with 26% in Germany, and integration remains shallow, concentrated in product development rather than in cross-cutting functions. This lag is above all organizational: 69% of French workers receive neither encouragement, nor tools, nor training in AI from their employer, compared with 44% in the United States. title: Politics at work: workplace experience and political divides among employees in France
text: Politics at work: workplace experience and political divides among employees in France LIFT Working Paper 2026-01 — February 2026 (first released as an HEC Policy Note) Democracy Work France Politics Published February 1, 2026 Abstract Drawing on a survey of 3,900 private-sector employees in 2024-2025, this note analyzes how everyday experience at work shapes political divides in France. The axis that separates electorates at work is neither wages nor socio-occupational category, but the quality of the social ties experienced day to day in the firm. Employees close to the Rassemblement National (RN) show strong trust in their firm but distrust their colleagues and are socially isolated, while employees close to La France insoumise (LFI) distrust management but trust their colleagues. One third of employees, the most isolated at work, are unaffiliated and do not vote: disengagement at work precedes civic disengagement. title: Cost of Failure, Disruptive Innovation and Targeted Flexicurity
text: Cost of Failure, Disruptive Innovation and Targeted Flexicurity LIFT Working Paper 2025-03 — October 2025 Innovation Europe Labor market Published October 1, 2025 Abstract This paper expands earlier work by assembling a larger sample of restructuring plans (250 plans) to measure the restructuring costs borne by large firms and to assess their links with business R&D in disruptive sectors (tech/biotech). The authors confirm a wide transatlantic gap, with Germany at 31 months of average salary versus 7 months in the United States, and identify low-cost outliers within Europe (Denmark, Switzerland). They show a strong negative correlation between restructuring costs and R&D intensity in tech and biotech, and conclude with recommendations for targeted reforms of employment protection laws that preserve social protection while restoring the agility critical for disruptive innovation. title: Artificial intelligence in the service of innovation: an analysis of patent data
text: Artificial intelligence in the service of innovation: an analysis of patent data LIFT Working Paper 2025-02 — July 2025 AI Innovation Published July 20, 2025 Abstract The impact of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies on economic growth depends largely on their ability to increase research productivity. In this article, we propose an original measure of the diffusion of AI across technologies, based on patents filed in the United States since 1990. Our methodology identifies patents that incorporate AI through their references to academic publications classified as AI. As of December 2024, about 5% of patents filed can thus be characterized as using AI. This approach captures the integration of AI into other technological fields, consistent with its nature as a general-purpose technology. We show that these “AI” patents systematically display higher quality indicators than other patents, according to several standard metrics in the literature. title: The diffusion of artificial intelligence in France
text: The diffusion of artificial intelligence in France LIFT Working Paper 2025-01 — July 2025 AI France Tracker Employment Published July 10, 2025 Abstract Using more than 120 million job postings published online in France since 2019, this study examines the characteristics of the diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI) in firms and its effects on employment. AI diffusion turns out to be highly heterogeneous: it is particularly advanced in certain sectors (IT, finance, consulting) and within large pioneering firms. This heterogeneity is also visible geographically, with AI job postings highly concentrated in employment zones that host research clusters or specialized industrial hubs (semiconductors, insurance, aeronautics, etc.). We show that the firms most exposed to AI were significantly more inclined to hire AI specialists as soon as ChatGPT appeared. At the same time, we observe a relative decline in job creation in the occupations most exposed to AI. However, hiring in AI occupations goes hand in hand with an increase in labor productivity and revenue, together with an increase in total employment in the firms concerned, driven by highly exposed occupations at the expense of less exposed ones. title: Exposure to generative artificial intelligence and employment: an application to the French socio-occupational classification
text: Exposure to generative artificial intelligence and employment: an application to the French socio-occupational classification LIFT Working Paper 2024-01 — January 2024 AI France Employment Published January 1, 2024 Abstract This paper analyzes the exposure of French occupations to generative artificial intelligence through the socio-occupational classification. Drawing on O*NET data and a GPT-4 assessment protocol, it proposes two indices: substitutability and complementarity. The results reveal strong heterogeneity across occupations, with higher exposure for the most skilled occupations. This approach helps to better identify automation risks and complementarity opportunities, and underscores the need to account for adoption costs and endogenous transformations to anticipate impacts on employment.
